summary: Extends Kerberos so a client can talk to a service without revealing its identity, or only its realm, and can get anonymous credentials from the key distribution center. It updates earlier Kerberos RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary:
Kerberos tickets normally say who they are for. This RFC adds a way to ask for a ticket that names nobody: an anonymous ticket.

There are two levels of hiding. The client can hide its identity from the service while still telling its own key distribution centre who it is. Or it can hide from both, by using a variant of the public-key exchange in which it signs nothing. Either way the ticket it receives is marked anonymous, so the client can check that it really got one before it uses it.

questions: how to get an anonymous kerberos ticket
what is the kerberos anonymous realm
subtitle: How a Kerberos client can prove who a server is without telling the server, or even the KDC, who the client is.

tldr.problem: A client may want to check that a service is genuine and protect the conversation, without disclosing who it is. Kerberos tickets always carry the client's name, so there was no way to ask for a ticket that named nobody.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an anonymous KDC option to the request, an anonymous ticket flag to the ticket, and a well-known anonymous realm and principal name. A client can hide its identity from the service, or hide it from its own key distribution centre as well, by asking for the ticket with anonymous PKINIT.
tldr.outcome: The client gets a ticket that names only the anonymous principal, which it uses to authenticate the server and protect what follows. The RFC obsoletes RFC 6112, which had errors and was not interoperable with any implementation.

today: RFC 8062 is a Proposed Standard from February 2017. It obsoletes RFC 6112 and reclassifies that document as Historic, because it contained errors and the protocol it described was not interoperable with any known implementation. It updates RFC 4120, RFC 4121 and RFC 4556.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In certain situations the Kerberos client may wish to authenticate a server and protect communications without revealing its own identity. For example, consider an application that provides read access to a research database and permits queries by arbitrary requesters. A client of such a service might wish to authenticate the service, to establish trust in the information received from it, but might not wish to disclose the client's identity to the service for privacy reasons.

The extensions specified here let a client authenticate the Key Distribution Center and request an anonymous ticket, and use that ticket to authenticate the server and protect subsequent client-server communications. The client may reveal its identity to its own KDC, or hide its identity completely by using anonymous PKINIT. Using the returned anonymous ticket, the client remains anonymous in subsequent Kerberos exchanges to KDCs on the cross-realm authentication path and to the server with which it communicates.

In this specification, the client realm in the anonymous ticket is the anonymous realm name when anonymous PKINIT is used to obtain the ticket, and the client's real realm name if the client is authenticated using the client's long-term keys. A membership in a realm can imply a member of the community represented by the realm.

This specification replaces RFC 6112 to correct technical errors in that specification. RFC 6112 is classified as Historic, and implementation of it is not recommended. The changes are small: the pepper string "KeyExchange" used in RFC 6112 is corrected to appear in all capital letters, to comply with the string actually used by implementations; the requirement for the anonymous option to be used in a TGS request is reduced from a MUST to a SHOULD; and the authorization data type name "AD-INITIAL-VERIFIED-CAS" is corrected to appear as "AD_INITIAL_VERIFIED_CAS".
sections.plainLanguage: The previous version of this document, RFC 6112, had mistakes in it and no implementation could talk to another. This one is the corrected version, and it is what real implementations follow.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.content:
The anonymous Kerberos realm name is a well-known realm name, and its value is the literal "WELLKNOWN:ANONYMOUS".

The anonymous Kerberos principal name is a well-known Kerberos principal name. The value of the name-type field is KRB_NT_WELLKNOWN, and the value of the name-string field is a sequence of two KerberosString components, "WELLKNOWN" and "ANONYMOUS".

The anonymous ticket flag is defined as bit 16, with the first bit being bit 0, in the TicketFlags. It is a new ticket flag used to indicate that a ticket is an anonymous one.

An anonymous ticket is a ticket that has all of the following properties. The cname field contains the anonymous Kerberos principal name. The crealm field contains the client's realm name or the anonymous realm name. The ticket contains no information that can reveal the client's identity, although it may contain the client realm, intermediate realms on the client's authentication path, and authorization data that may provide information related to the client's identity: an anonymous principal that is identifiable only as being in a particular group of users can be implemented using authorization data, and such data would disclose that the client is a member of the group observed. And the anonymous ticket flag is set.

The anonymous KDC option is defined as bit 16 in the KDCOptions, and is set to request an anonymous ticket in an Authentication Service request or a Ticket-Granting Service request.
sections.plainLanguage: Four names and bits carry the whole mechanism: a realm called WELLKNOWN:ANONYMOUS, a principal called WELLKNOWN ANONYMOUS, one bit in the ticket that says it is anonymous, and one bit in the request that asks for one.

sections.title: Anonymity in the AS Exchange
sections.content:
To request an anonymous ticket, the client sets the anonymous KDC option in an AS exchange. The client can use its long-term keys, its X.509 certificates, or any other pre-authentication data to authenticate to the KDC and request an anonymous ticket in an AS exchange where the client's identity is known to the KDC.

If the client in the AS request is anonymous, the anonymous KDC option must be set in the request; otherwise the KDC must return a KRB-ERROR with the code KDC_ERR_BADOPTION. If the client is anonymous and the KDC does not have a key to encrypt the reply, which can happen for example when the KDC does not support PKINIT, the KDC must return an error with the code KDC_ERR_NULL_KEY.

When policy allows, the KDC issues an anonymous ticket. If the client name in the request is the anonymous principal, the client realm in the reply is the anonymous realm; otherwise the client realm is the realm of the AS. The KDC must not reveal the client's identity in the authorization data of the returned ticket. The AD_INITIAL_VERIFIED_CAS authorization data contains the issuer name of the client certificate; it is not applicable and must not be present in the returned anonymous ticket when anonymous PKINIT is used. When the client is authenticated by other means, if it is undesirable to disclose information about the client's identity, that authorization data should be removed from the returned anonymous ticket.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting one bit in the request asks for an anonymous ticket. The KDC can still refuse, and if it agrees it must strip anything from the ticket that would give the client away.

sections.title: Anonymous PKINIT
sections.content:
Without revealing its identity to the KDC, the client can request an anonymous ticket by setting the client name as the anonymous principal in the AS exchange and providing PA_PK_AS_REQ pre-authentication data where the signerInfos field of the SignedData is empty and the certificates field is absent. Because the anonymous client does not have an associated asymmetric key pair, the client must choose the Diffie-Hellman key agreement method by filling in the Diffie-Hellman domain parameters in the clientPublicValue. This use of the anonymous client name in conjunction with PKINIT is referred to as anonymous PKINIT. If anonymous PKINIT is used, the realm name in the returned anonymous ticket must be the anonymous realm.

On receiving an anonymous PKINIT request, the KDC processes the request normally but skips the checks for the client's signature and the client's public key, such as the verification of the binding between the client's public key and the client name. The AS must check that the client's Diffie-Hellman domain parameters are acceptable, and the Diffie-Hellman key agreement method must be used. If the clientPublicValue is not present, the KDC must return a KRB-ERROR with the code KDC_ERR_PUBLIC_KEY_ENCRYPTION_NOT_SUPPORTED. If all goes well, an anonymous ticket is generated and PA_PK_AS_REP pre-authentication data is included in the reply. If the KDC does not have an asymmetric key pair, it may reply anonymously or reject the attempt; if it replies anonymously, the signerInfos field of the PA_PK_AS_REP is empty and the certificates field is absent.

Upon receipt of a KDC reply containing an anonymous ticket and PA_PK_AS_REP, the client can authenticate the KDC based on the KDC's signature. If that signature is missing, the client must reject the returned ticket if it cannot authenticate the KDC otherwise. A KDC that supports anonymous PKINIT must indicate the support of PKINIT, and must indicate support for anonymous PKINIT by including a padata element of padata-type PA_PKINIT_KX with an empty padata-value when including PA-PK-AS-REQ in an error reply.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the strong version. The client signs nothing and sends no certificate, so the key distribution centre never learns who it is. The exchange still produces a key both sides hold, so the ticket is still protected.

sections.title: Anonymity in the TGS Exchange
sections.content:
The client requests an anonymous ticket by setting the anonymous KDC option in a TGS exchange, and in that request it can use a normal Ticket-Granting Ticket with the client's identity, an anonymous TGT, or an anonymous cross-realm TGT. If the client uses a normal TGT, the client's identity is known to the TGS. If the ticket in the PA-TGS-REQ of the TGS request is an anonymous one, the anonymous KDC option should be set in the request.

When policy allows, the KDC issues an anonymous ticket. If the ticket in the TGS request is an anonymous one, the client name and the client realm are copied from that ticket; otherwise the returned anonymous ticket contains the client name as the anonymous principal and the client realm as the true realm of the client.

The TGS must not reveal the client's identity in the authorization data of the returned ticket, and must process the authorization data recursively so that all embedded elements are interpreted. It should not populate identity-based authorization data into an anonymous ticket. Where an authorization data element may reveal the client's identity it must be removed unless otherwise specified. Where such an element is intended to restrict the use of the ticket or limit the rights otherwise conveyed in the ticket, it cannot be removed in order to hide the client's identity, and the authentication attempt must be rejected with the code KDC_ERR_POLICY. Where an element is unknown, the TGS may remove it, transfer it, or reject the attempt, based on local policy; if there is no policy defined for a given unknown authorization data type, the authentication must be rejected with KDC_ERR_POLICY.

The TGS encodes the name of the previous realm into the transited field. Based on local policy it may omit the previous realm if the cross-realm TGT is an anonymous one, in order to hide the authentication path of the client. The anonymous Kerberos realm name must not be present in the transited field of a ticket, while the true name of the realm that issued the anonymous ticket may be.
sections.plainLanguage: The same idea applies when the client already holds a ticket. The tricky part is the extra information in the ticket: if some piece of it restricts what the ticket may be used for, it cannot be quietly removed, so the request has to be refused instead.

sections.title: Interoperability and GSS-API Notes
sections.content:
Conforming implementations must support the anonymous principal with a non-anonymous realm, and may support the anonymous principal with the anonymous realm using anonymous PKINIT.

GSS-API defines the name_type GSS_C_NT_ANONYMOUS to represent the anonymous identity. The anonymous principal with the anonymous realm corresponds to the GSS-API anonymous principal. A principal with the anonymous principal name and a non-anonymous realm is an authenticated principal, so it does not correspond to the anonymous principal in GSS-API with the GSS_C_NT_ANONYMOUS name type, and the name syntax for GSS_KRB5_NT_PRINCIPAL_NAME must be used for importing, displaying and exporting such names.

At the GSS-API level, an initiator requests the use of an anonymous principal with the anonymous realm by asserting the "anonymous" flag when calling GSS_Init_Sec_Context. A GSS-API initiator must carefully check the resulting context attributes from the initial call to GSS_Init_Sec_Context when requesting anonymity, because anonymity is just another optional context attribute. The mechanism might not recognize the attribute at all, or anonymity might not be available for other reasons, and in that case the initiator must not send the initial security context token to the acceptor, because it will likely reveal the initiator's identity to the acceptor, something that can rarely be undone.
sections.plainLanguage: The GSS-API layer has its own way of saying "anonymous", and it is only a hint. If the library cannot honour it, the client must stop before it has sent anything, because the first token already carries the identity.

sections.title: The KDC Contribution to the Ticket Session Key
sections.content:
The definition in this section was motivated by protocol analysis of anonymous PKINIT in building secure channels. In order to enable applications of anonymous PKINIT to form secure channels, all implementations of anonymous PKINIT need to meet its requirements.

PKINIT is useful for constructing secure channels. To ensure that an active attacker cannot create separate channels to the client and the KDC with the same known key, it is desirable that neither the KDC nor the client unilaterally determine the ticket session key. A KDC conforming to this definition must encrypt a randomly generated key, called the KDC contribution key, in the PA_PKINIT_KX padata. The KDC contribution key is then combined with the reply key to form the ticket session key of the returned ticket. The two keys are combined using the KRB-FX-CF2 operation, where K1 is the KDC contribution key, K2 is the reply key, the input pepper1 is the US-ASCII string "PKINIT" and the input pepper2 is the US-ASCII string "KEYEXCHANGE".

The PA_PKINIT_KX padata must be included in the KDC reply when anonymous PKINIT is used, should be included if PKINIT is used with the Diffie-Hellman key exchange but the client is not anonymous, and must not be included otherwise. The padata-value field contains the DER encoding of the PA-PKINIT-KX type, which is an EncryptedData whose cleartext is the DER-encoded KDC contribution key randomly generated by the KDC. The encryption key is the reply key, and the key usage number is KEY_USAGE_PA_PKINIT_KX, which is 44.

The client then decrypts the KDC contribution key and verifies that the ticket session key in the returned ticket is the combined key of the KDC contribution key and the reply key. A conforming client must reject anonymous PKINIT authentication if the PA_PKINIT_KX padata is not present in the KDC reply, or if the ticket session key is not the combined key when it is present.
sections.plainLanguage: Without this, an attacker in the middle could run two separate Diffie-Hellman exchanges and read the ticket. Requiring both sides to contribute a piece of the session key means the client can check that the ticket it received really belongs to the exchange it ran.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since KDCs ignore unknown options, a client requiring anonymous communication needs to make sure that the returned ticket is actually anonymous, because a KDC that does not understand the anonymous option would not return one. The client must therefore check for the anonymous ticket flag in the flags field of the EncKDCRepPart before using the ticket, otherwise the client's identity may be revealed unintentionally.

By using the mechanism defined here, the client does not reveal its identity to the server, but the client's identity may be revealed to the KDC of the server principal, when the server principal is in a different realm than the client, and to any KDC on the cross-realm authentication path.

If a KDC that issued an anonymous ticket were to maintain records of the association of identities to an anonymous ticket, then someone obtaining such records could breach the anonymity. The implementations of most, currently all, KDCs respond to requests at the time they are received, so traffic analysis on the connection to the KDC will allow an attacker to match client identities to anonymous tickets issued. Because there are plaintext parts of the tickets exposed on the wire, such matching by a third-party observer is relatively straightforward. A service authenticated by the anonymous principals may also be able to infer the identity of the client by examining and linking quasi-static protocol information such as the IP address from which a request is received, or by linking multiple uses of the same anonymous ticket.

Two mechanisms, the FAST facility with the hide-client-names option and the Kerberos5 starttls option, protect the client identity so that an attacker would never be able to observe the client identity sent to the KDC. Transport- or network-layer security between the client and the server helps prevent tracking of a particular ticket, and clients can limit how often a ticket is reused to minimize ticket linking.

Application servers may reject the authentication in order to prevent information disclosure or as part of denial-of-service prevention, and must avoid accepting anonymous credentials in situations where they must record the client's identity, for example when there must be an audit trail.
sections.plainLanguage: Anonymous to the service is not the same as anonymous to everyone. The key distribution centre still sees who asked, and someone watching the network can often work it out from the traffic. The RFC lists the ways to reduce that.

viz.caption: The names and bits that carry the mechanism

items.title: Anonymous principal name
items.text: Name type KRB_NT_WELLKNOWN, with the name string made of the two components WELLKNOWN and ANONYMOUS.

items.title: Anonymous ticket flag
items.text: Bit 16 in the TicketFlags field. It is set on a ticket that is anonymous.

items.title: Anonymous KDC option
items.text: Bit 16 in the KDCOptions field. It is set in a request to ask for an anonymous ticket.

viz.caption: Getting and using an anonymous ticket, illustrative, not from the RFC

messages.label: AS-REQ with the anonymous option
messages.note: The client asks for an anonymous ticket, either identifying itself to the KDC or hiding its identity with anonymous PKINIT.

messages.label: AS-REP with an anonymous ticket
messages.note: The KDC issues the ticket, with the anonymous client name and a client realm, and with anything identifying the client removed.

messages.label: AP-REQ using the anonymous ticket
messages.note: The client authenticates the server and protects the session without giving its identity away.

viz.caption: Anonymous PKINIT against an ordinary AS exchange

cells: What the client proves to the KDC
Nothing; there is no signature and no certificate
Its identity, with a long-term key or a certificate
Diffie-Hellman, which the client must choose
The signature and public key checks

items.label: PA_PKINIT_KX
items.desc: Pre-authentication data that carries an encrypted KDC contribution key.

items.label: KEY_USAGE_PA_PKINIT_KX
items.desc: The key usage number used when the KDC encrypts the contribution key.

items.label: Bad option
items.desc: Returned when the client in an AS request is anonymous but did not set the anonymous KDC option.

items.label: No key for the reply
items.desc: Returned when the client is anonymous and the KDC has no key to encrypt the reply with.

items.label: Policy
items.desc: Returned when authorization data that restricts the ticket's use cannot be removed without revealing the client's identity.
